body.text: First Nations advocates call for national approach to invasive species at COP31
In short:
First Nations advocates have told COP31 invasive species are threatening Australia's biodiversity and cultural heritage.
An all-female First Nations delegation attended the summit in Türkiye, which finishes this weekend.
What's next:
The federal government will decide whether to list buffel grass as a Weed of National Significance next month.
First Nations advocates have taken their fight against invasive species to the global stage, just weeks before the federal government will decide whether to list buffel grass as a national weed.
Kalkadoon woman Taigen Ryan, a campaign lead for the Invasive Species Council, took part in the annual COP 31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.
She said her message was focused on the threat buffel grass posed to native flora and fauna as well as Australia's unique Indigenous cultural heritage.
"It's such a massive fire risk. It pushes out our native wildlife and creates monocultures which are not good for the biodiversity of our land," Ms Ryan told the ABC from Antalya.
"Buffel grass is such a flammable, invasive weed … so there's risks to communities, to Country, to species, all of the above."
Ms Ryan was part of an all-female First Nations delegation in Antalya.
It was put together by Common Threads, an Indigenous advocacy organisation, with the aim of raising concerns about climate change through an Indigenous lens.
Buffel grass was introduced to Australia in the late 1800s as fodder for livestock and to control soil erosion and dust storms.
It's still widely used and lauded by the pastoral industry, particularly in drier parts of the country.
Since its introduction, the hardy and drought-tolerant grass has spread across every mainland state and territory except the ACT.
The Northern Territory and South Australia governments have declared buffel grass a weed and implemented their own management strategies.
In 2025 buffel was nominated by Indigenous and environmental groups for listing as a "Weed of National Significance".
A decision is set to be made by the National Biosecurity Committee in December.
Ms Ryan said a listing would make the management and control of buffel grass a national priority.
"We really need that coordinated response and national funding to tackle the issue at scale," she said.
The Northern Territory Cattleman's Association (NTCA) opposed the nomination, saying buffel grass is "a cornerstone of Australian red meat production and food security".
The ABC has contacted the NTCA for comment.
Impact on sacred sites

Central Australia — with its vast swathes of largely-uninhabited countryside, and often the home of Aboriginal-owned land or giant cattle stations — is quickly shaping up as ground zero for the conversation about buffel grass.
In and around Alice Springs, Arrernte country, buffel is omnipresent.
Garth Forrester, regional land management co-ordinator with the Central Land Council, said he had seen first-hand how culture was impacted by the spread of buffel.

"Our mob, a hundred years ago, would've been able to navigate the country like this. They'd be able to walk through and hunt and look for animals and actually look at the tracks that they could follow to navigate the country," he said.
"Whereas [with] the buffel grass, you can see how pushed together they are, how they group together and how it overtakes and just a simple thing like a fire would change this whole ecosystem.
"I hate to say it, but our mob a hundred years ago would be lost, they wouldn't be able to navigate this country."
The Central Arrernte, Luritja and Pitjantjara man has been a ranger for 30 years.
He supports two ranger groups and helps manage the Katiti-Petermann Indigenous Protected Area surrounding Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park.
Mr Forrester said in his line of work simply traversing country has risks of encouraging the spread of buffel, especially to culturally significant areas known as sacred sites.

"If there's a sacred site on the other side and I wanted to drive my vehicle through or walk through, there's a fair chance I'm going to be taking a few of those buffel seeds from this space to the other side," he said.
It meant cars and clothing had to be thoroughly inspected, he said.
"If you have to do a lot of work just to go visit a place, you're better off staying away until it's more manageable."
Mr Forrester said many plants and animals had totemic or ceremonial value, and that iconography was being threatened.
"The buffel grass is starting to hide a lot of these natives. The natives might be dormant underground, but you can't see it if it's being covered," he said.
He said younger generations then missed out learning about traditional plants and bush foods.
"Don't forget that plants and animals are tied together," he said.
"Everything is related in this world, even a small insect has a name, it's got a meaning, it has its own dreaming story on this Earth.
"Plants, even bush potatoes and berries have a dreaming, have a name, have a culture, have a song, have a story. These things are very old."
